```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.5, fig.align = "center",
                      dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
```

Many learning settings involve more than two kinds of actor. A student
working with an AI assistant inside a programming environment interacts with
the assistant and with the environment itself, whose compiler messages,
notifications and logs are events of a third kind. A classroom dialogue can
involve a teacher, students and a conversational agent. Heterogeneous
transition network analysis does not depend on there being two actors: the
actor partition can have any number of groups, and the weight matrix is then
partitioned into one block for every ordered pair of actors. With three
actors there are three within-actor blocks and six between-actor blocks, so
the question of who hands over to whom has six answers instead of two.

This guide builds a three-actor network, reads its actor-pair structure,
draws it in the layouts available for several groups, counts the
three-actor meta-paths, and compares two networks. Every function used for
two actors works unchanged.

```{r package}
library(htna)
```

## Data

The package has no bundled data with three actor types, so the guide uses a
small simulated study of 30 sessions in which a Student, an AI assistant and
a System (the programming environment) act in turn. Each actor has four
codes.

- **Student**: `Ask`, `Confirm`, `Revise`, `Evaluate`.
- **AI**: `Suggest`, `Explain`, `Execute`, `Clarify`.
- **System**: `Log`, `Notify`, `Compile`, `Sync`.
- **Session and order**: `session_id` and `order_in_session`. In each
  session the three actors act in the fixed cycle Student, AI, System for as
  long as each has events (15 to 25 per actor and session), and the codes
  within an actor are drawn at random.

The turn order is therefore built into the data, and the codes carry no
structure. The analyses below should recover the cycle and nothing else.

```{r simulate}
set.seed(42)
student_codes <- c("Ask", "Confirm", "Revise", "Evaluate")
ai_codes      <- c("Suggest", "Explain", "Execute", "Clarify")
system_codes  <- c("Log", "Notify", "Compile", "Sync")
sessions      <- sprintf("S%03d", seq_len(30))

make_events <- function(codes, sessions, offset) {
  rows <- lapply(sessions, function(sid) {
    n <- sample(15:25, 1)
    data.frame(session_id = sid, code = sample(codes, n, replace = TRUE),
               order_in_session = seq_len(n) * 3L - offset)
  })
  do.call(rbind, rows)
}

student_data <- make_events(student_codes, sessions, 2L)
ai_data      <- make_events(ai_codes, sessions, 1L)
system_data  <- make_events(system_codes, sessions, 0L)
```

## Building a network with three actors

The three tables are passed as a named list; the names become the actor
types, in the order given. A single table with an actor column or a
codebook works in the same way (see [Input formats](input-formats.html)).

```{r build}
net3 <- build_htna(list(Student = student_data, AI = ai_data,
                        System = system_data))
summary(net3)
```

The network has 12 nodes, four per actor, and 116 of its 144 possible edges
are non-zero. The edge counts by actor form a three-by-three table. As a
tidy table, one row per directed actor pair:

```{r actor-pairs}
as.data.frame(summary(net3), what = "actor_pairs")
```

The block structure reflects the turn cycle: the Student-to-Student block
has only 3 non-zero edges, because a student event is followed by another
student event only where the other actors have run out of events, while the
blocks of the cycle (Student to AI, AI to System, System to Student) have 16
each, all possible edges. The other blocks are filled at the ends of
sessions, where the remaining actors continue among themselves.

## Drawing three actor groups

With the default circular layout each actor occupies one arc of the circle,
coloured and shaped by actor.

```{r plot-circle}
plot_htna(net3)
```

`layout = "polygon"` places each actor along one side of a regular polygon,
a triangle for three actors, which separates the groups more clearly.

```{r plot-polygon}
plot_htna(net3, layout = "polygon")
```

## Which three-actor templates recur?

`extract_meta_paths()` at the type level counts runs of actor types. With
three actors there are 27 possible templates of length three.

```{r meta-type}
print(extract_meta_paths(net3, level = "type", length = 3), n = 6)
```

The three rotations of the cycle (`Student->AI->System`,
`AI->System->Student`, `System->Student->AI`) occur in all 30 sessions and
account for 0.295, 0.288 and 0.282 of the runs, about eight times as often
as expected from the actors' overall shares (lift 7.62 to 7.98). The next
most frequent template, `AI->System->AI`, occurs 41 times in 10 sessions,
less often than expected (lift 0.62). The
meta-paths recover the built-in turn order exactly. A schema returns the
concrete instances of one template:

```{r meta-schema}
print(extract_meta_paths(net3, schema = "Student->AI->System"), n = 6)
```

All 64 combinations of four codes per actor occur, and because the codes
within each actor were drawn at random they have similar counts (the most
frequent, `Confirm->Clarify->Compile`, occurs 15 times); no particular
student move leads to a particular AI move. Their high lifts come from the
turn cycle, not from the codes.

## Do two samples from the same process differ?

A second set of 30 sessions is simulated from the same process. A
permutation test of the two networks should find no difference.

```{r second-sample}
set.seed(7)
net3b <- build_htna(list(
  Student = make_events(student_codes, sessions, 2L),
  AI      = make_events(ai_codes, sessions, 1L),
  System  = make_events(system_codes, sessions, 0L)
))
perm3 <- permutation_htna(net3, net3b, iter = 200, seed = 1)
perm3
```

The global test finds no difference (M = 2.693, p = 0.587; S = 0.103,
p = 0.846), and 2 of the 136 tested edges fall below 0.05, fewer than the
seven expected by chance at that level. The test behaves as it should when
the two networks come from one process. The difference network draws the
two nominally significant edges:

```{r diff-plot}
plot_htna_diff(perm3)
```

With `show_nonsig = TRUE`, the non-significant differences are added as
dashed edges.

```{r diff-plot-all}
plot_htna_diff(perm3, show_nonsig = TRUE)
```

## What changes with more actors

| Step | Two actors | Three or more actors |
|---|---|---|
| Actor-pair blocks | 4 | the number of actors squared (9 for three) |
| Layout | circular, two arcs | circular arcs, or `layout = "polygon"` |
| Meta-paths of length three | 8 templates | the number of actors cubed (27 for three) |
| Comparison and assessment | `compare_htna()`, `permutation_htna()`, `bootstrap_htna()` | unchanged |

The number of blocks and templates grows quickly with the number of actors,
so more sessions are needed to estimate every block; the actor-pair table of
`summary()` shows which blocks rest on few edges.
